# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–31 (Complete – Updated 2026-10-13)

## Setting and Time
- **Current Period**: Autumn of eighth year after Waterloo (1830). Earlier sections covered spring through summer; now autumn.
- **Locations**: London (Welbeck Street, Grosvenor Square, Abchurch Lane, Beargarden Club, Langham Hotel, Euston Square Railway Station); Coventry Island; Queen's Crawley; Coldcombe and Mirecombe farms; Bryngate; Pumpernickel; Ostend; Hampshire ("the Evergreens"); Brussels; Aix-la-Chapelle; Bath and Cheltenham; Carbury Hall; Carbury Chase; Beccles; Quenwick; Harrowgate; Dunwick; Liverpool; San Francisco; California; Salt Lake City; New Mexico; Arizona; Mexico; Vera Cruz; Queenstown.

## Major Deaths
- **John Sedley**: Died peacefully; buried at Brompton.
- **Mr. Osborne**: Deceased (four days after stroke); Major Dobbin appointed executor; Georgy established as heir.
- **Joseph Sedley**: Died at Aix-la-Chapelle three months after Dobbin's final visit. Heavily insured (£2,000); legacy split equally between Amelia and Rebecca (administratrix).
- **Colonel Rawdon Crawley**: Died of yellow fever at Coventry Island; estate devolved upon Sir Pitt's son, now Sir Rawdon Crawley, Bart.
- **Sir Pitt**: Died six weeks after Colonel Rawdon.

## Rebecca's Arc
**Seduction and Enslavement of Jos Sedley**: At Pumpernickel, Rebecca (Madame de Raudon, formerly with Rawdon Crawley) seduced Jos through calculated performance. Led him to Room No. 92, Elephant lodging-house. Within week, Jos became her "entirely slave." Lived in Brussels hotel in genteel manner. Jos died three months later at Aix-la-Chapelle. Insurance company challenged £2,000 payment; Rebecca prevailed. **Dobbin sent back his share and rigidly declined communication.**

**Final State**: Never became Lady Crawley though styles herself so. Son (Sir Rawdon, young baronet) declines to see her; receives liberal allowance. Appears very wealthy. Chiefly at Bath and Cheltenham; strong party considers her "most injured woman." Busies herself in piety, church attendance, Charity Lists.

## Amelia and William Dobbin
**Resolution**: At Ostend, Becky revealed George Osborne was "selfish humbug, low-bred cockney dandy" who wanted her to run away with him—"Dobbin forced him to keep his word." Emmy's internal struggle resolved: "There is nothing to forbid me now...I may love him with all my heart now."

**Marriage and Life**: Two mornings later at Dike, Amelia went to Dobbin "in dripping white bonnet and shawl...kissing one of his hands with all her might." Only Georgy and Jos present. Emmy told William: "Never speak of that day again." Dobbin quit service immediately, rented "the Evergreens" (Hampshire). Devoted father; fonder of daughter Jane (christened by Rev. James Crawley) than of his History of the Punjaub. Lady Jane godmother to daughter; they became great friends.

## Lady Carbury and Family

**Lady Carbury**: Lives modestly on Welbeck Street with son Felix and daughter Henrietta. "The woman was false from head to foot, but there was much of good in her, false though she was." Devoted to children, especially Felix. Back drawing-room serves as workspace for writing books and contriving systems for editors and critics.

**Felix Carbury** (son): Beautiful as a star; cynosure of mother's eyes. Mother spoilt him; almost proud of his vices. Won £2,000 from Lord Grasslough and £400 from Miles Grendall at gaming (retained winnings). **Currently considering courtship of Marie Melmotte (great heiress); at Melmotte ball, waltzes with Marie, studying words ("I do") to convince her he could love her.** Since Roger's offer to Henrietta, Felix "gone on from bad to worse, till his condition had become one of hopeless embarrassment." Despite debts, claims to be "all right"; boasts money in pocket. Roger suspects talk of giving home for Henrietta is delusional. Felix lacks courage to shake off Roger violently; dreads Roger's words with "craven fear." **Now director of South Central Pacific and Mexican Railway Company.** **Gambling at Beargarden has gone on with little interruption; on whole keeps his luck with vicissitudes. Miles Grendall suggested to Lord Grasslough foul play; Grasslough repudiated idea. Miles watched in vain; Sir Felix not yet a blackleg. Miles, Grasslough, and Dolly Longestaffe all owe Sir Felix considerable sums of money. Lately very little ready money passed hands—mostly written documents.**

**Henrietta Carbury** (daughter): Romance with cousin Roger Carbury (of Carbury Hall, nearly forty) and Paul Montague. Roger offered hand passionately. Paul fell in love during second visit to Carbury Hall. Hot-worded scene between Roger and Paul lasted above an hour; Paul packed and was driven to railway station by Roger without seeing either lady, departing in tears. Roger blessed him at platform. **Henrietta rejected Roger's suit, claiming too young and age disparity insurmountable; admitted "even that disparity was not now her strongest reason."** Within week, Paul returned "as a still dear friend," having promised not to see Henrietta for three months but nothing further. Paul doubts his finances (share in "doubtful business of Fisker, Montague, and Montague, 250 miles further off than San Francisco") but declared he has money and won't give up Henrietta on account of finances. Roger will not accede to justice of Paul's argument.

**Lady Carbury's Divided Concerns**: Solicitude for son greatly increases desire for daughter's union with Roger. Roger came to London horrified that man with no income has hunters. Roger recommended Lady Carbury give up town house, find home for daughter elsewhere, let Felix "bear the brunt of his own misdoings." Roger believes remedy lies in mother's conduct: were she not foolishly weak, she would divide utterly from son and leave him to suffer utter penury. **Roger remains firmly opposed to Melmotte connection on principle; holds old-fashioned idea that "touching of pitch will defile."** Roger resolved to warn Henrietta against Melmotte.

## The Melmottes

**Augustus Melmotte, Esq.**: Arrived in London from Paris within last two years; previously M. Melmotte. Claims English birth though speaks native language fluently with accent betraying "long expatriation." In City, his name "worth any money." Big man with large whiskers, rough hair, expression of mental power on harsh vulgar face; repellent unless attracted by internal consideration. Magnificent in expenditure, successful in business. **Miles Grendall serves as his usher/secretary in office.** **Chairman of South Central Pacific and Mexican Railway Company with two million dollars of shares allocated to himself.**

**Madame Melmotte**: Said to have been Bohemian Jewess; speaks very little English.

**Marie Melmotte**: Spoke as Mademoiselle Marie; now speaks English well as foreigner. **Has begun forming own opinions; absolutely rejected Lord Grasslough (bankrupt, no income, ugly, vicious, ill-tempered).** Had experience with Lord Nidderdale. **People saying if Sir Felix Carbury managed affairs well he might be the happy man.**

## South Central Pacific and Mexican Railway Scheme

**The Enterprise**: Grand proposal for railway from Salt Lake City, branching from San Francisco and Chicago line, passing through fertile lands of New Mexico and Arizona into Mexican Republic, running by city of Mexico, terminating at Vera Cruz. **Distance approximately 2,000 miles; no computation made as to probable cost.** Fisker considers such questions "beside the mark and childish." Concession obtained from United States Government; correspondence maintained with President of Mexican Republic.

**Financial Strategy**: Stock to be taken "at par"; shares to be sold at premium. Goal to "run them up even to 110," yielding three hundred thousand dollars minimum. **None of the directors believed they were really making a railway; instead, they understood their fortune would be made by floating railway shares—advertising people out of doors into buying shares while those "indoors" manufactured the shares to be sold. All whispered to each other their convictions on this.**

**Key Players**:
- **Hamilton K. Fisker**: American, approximately forty. Partner in Fisker, Montague, and Montague (San Francisco). Small, shining man with well-twisted moustache, greasy brown hair balding at top. Gorgeously dressed with silk waistcoat, chains, carries little stick. Troubled by no shyness, scruples, or fears. Supremely confident, good-humoured, audacious, clever. Previously engaged in California financing. **Made fluent, fast, florid speech before Melmotte about world-wide commercial harmony to be produced by railway; his words were less effective than one ponderous word from Melmotte's mouth. Fisker's arms waved gracefully; head turned this way and that, never towards his plate.** **At cardroom gaming at Beargarden, suggested poker as desirable pastime; when Lord Nidderdale objected citing poetry about "Heathen Chinee," Fisker declared himself ready for any game irrespective of religious prejudices.** **Extracted from Sir Felix small documents bearing M. G. notation indicating debts owed; also extracted one for Dolly Longestaffe's £50 indebtedness; produced documents showing Felix owed Grasslough £150, Nidderdale £145, Grendall £322 10s. Fisker behaved with perfect good humour about money, extracted cheque from Herr Vossner for lords' debts, then took affectionate leave, saying "One cheer for the South Central Pacific and Mexican Railway" as he departed.** **Not one present had liked Fisker—his manners, waistcoat, smoking style, spitting on carpet were all offensive; said "my lord" too often; grated prejudices equally whether treating with familiarity or deference. But he had behaved well about money, making them feel they were behaving badly.**

- **Paul Montague**: Junior member of firm. English. Personally dislikes Fisker but unable to resist his combination of good humour, audacity, cleverness. Trembles for his money; wishes never to see Fisker again. Obeyed Fisker's telegram order to meet at Liverpool immediately. Met Fisker at great railway hotel; Fisker displayed maps, schedules, printed programmes. **Letter dated from Langham Hotel, posted at Euston Square Railway Station, invited Melmotte to meet; following morning Paul and Fisker travelled to London together.** Fisker presented himself in Abchurch Lane office; resulted in twenty-minute wait before audience with Melmotte granted.

**Launch and Direction**: **At end of fortnight from Fisker's arrival, company fully launched with body of London directors, of whom Melmotte is chairman. Among directors: Lord Alfred Grendall, Sir Felix Carbury, Samuel Cohenlupe, Esq. (Member of Parliament for Staines, Jewish persuasion), Lord Nidderdale, and Paul Montague.** Fisker fully satisfied. Melmotte's telegraph and close inquiries made scheme seem real; though many thought him "built upon the sands." **Paul took to living good deal at Beargarden; reasoned man dines cheaper at club. Saw good deal of brother directors Sir Felix and Lord Nidderdale; entertained Lord Alfred once; dined twice with Melmotte amidst merchant-princely hospitality in Grosvenor Square. Fisker suggested Paul enter himself for great Marie Melmotte plate. Greatness of operations relieved Fisker and Montague from necessity of looking to small expenses; champagne consumption increased, deleterious results. Montague found he could not wake up on London mornings with satisfactory thoughts as at old Manor House (Carbury Hall).** **At Beargarden cardroom, Montague offered to undertake Grendall's debt himself; this could not be allowed—he had only lately come among them, had no dealing in I.O.U.'s, and was last man who ought to be made responsible for Grendall's impecuniosity.**

## Roger Carbury
Nearly forty years old. Never owed shilling he could not pay; father likewise. Carbury parish named for family. Carbury Chase (partly in Carbury parish, partly Bundlesham) belongs unfortunately in entirety to Bundlesham estate.

## Miscellaneous Plot Elements (Chapter 31)
**Harrowgate**: Fedette Orlwood broke faith with Madrek Orlwood; promised work to rebuild fallen wall at Harrowgate never begun.

**Dunwick**: Conar Hollett gave solemn promise to repair roof of chapel at Dunwick.

**Mirecombe Hill Farms**: Setting includes Aewyn Brackwood and Conar Hollett; autumn weather with question of rain.
